Excessive exercise does not clearly serve or connect to those symptoms, making it look like a strategy for a different presentation unless additional context were present.

issues.item: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Life Not Worth Living' is disproportionately severe relative to the rest of the selected profile and is not well supported by the surrounding appraisals. The other appraisals focus on danger and bodily unreliability, while the threat/memory items emphasize hyperarousal and fragmented recall. This suicidal-hopelessness appraisal can occur in PTSD, but here it stands out as insufficiently linked to the rest of the formulation and item set.

vignette:
# Mariana

Mariana was twenty-two when the bomb went off at the transit hub downtown. She had been standing in line at the coffee kiosk, waiting for her shift at the warehouse to start, when the blast came—a sound so complete it seemed to erase everything before it. The percussion threw her backward. Her ears rang with a frequency that felt like it was coming from inside her own skull. Around her, people screamed, but their voices sounded distant, muffled, as though she were underwater. She remembered the smell—acrid, chemical, mixed with something burnt and organic that she could not name. She remembered running, her legs moving without her consent, her body taking over while her mind seemed to fracture into separate pieces. There were gaps in what came after: she could not recall how she got out of the building, could not picture the faces of the people she must have passed, could not remember the exact moment she realized she was bleeding from a cut on her shoulder. When she tried to fill in those blanks later, in the safety of her apartment, the effort made her feel as though she were drowning all over again.

The months that followed were a slow erosion. What frightened Mariana most was that she had come to believe the world was fundamentally dangerous—that the randomness of that day was not an aberration but a glimpse of reality. If it could happen at a coffee kiosk on an ordinary Tuesday, it could happen anywhere. This conviction fed her need to be constantly on guard, scanning every room the moment she entered it, noting exits, watching the hands and bodies of people around her. On the drive to work, when her vigilance was highest and her sense of threat most acute, the memory would surface unbidden—the sound, the acrid smell, the fracturing sensation—pulled to the surface by the very alertness she was using to protect herself, as though her mind needed to keep reviewing what had happened to stay one step ahead of the next disaster. Because she had concluded that danger was everywhere and she was powerless to predict it, the strategies she adopted—the watching, the positioning near exits, the deliberate disconnection—were not anxious habits but rational survival measures, the only tools available to someone living in a fundamentally hostile world. At the warehouse, where she had worked for three years, her hypervigilance became a visible thing. She positioned herself near the loading dock, away from crowds of coworkers. She tracked the movements of the forklift operators obsessively, her body tensing whenever someone moved too quickly or unexpectedly. Her supervisor had begun to notice. She was making mistakes—missing inventory counts because she was too busy watching the perimeter—and her coworkers had started giving her a wide berth, unsettled by the intensity of her gaze, the way she flinched if someone approached from her blind side.

The gaps in her memory of the event felt like proof that her own body had betrayed her. She knew, in a factual way, that she had survived, that she had made it out, but she could not locate herself within the narrative of those missing minutes. This absence terrified her because it suggested her body might fail her again without warning. She no longer trusted it to protect her or to respond correctly in a crisis. When she tried to talk to her sister about what had happened, the words simply would not come. She knew the sequence of events—the sound, the fall, the running—but when she opened her mouth to describe it, something seized in her throat. The only feeling that came through clearly was rage, a burning fury at the randomness, at her own helplessness, at the fact that she had survived when others had not. That rage would surge without warning, often triggered by small things: a car backfiring, a door slamming, a sudden movement in her peripheral vision. In those moments, she felt as though she might explode, and the intensity of the anger terrified her almost as much as the fear itself.

To manage the constant threat she perceived, Mariana began to deliberately disconnect from her body and her surroundings. She would sit in the break room at work and practice a kind of deliberate blankness, letting her mind drift to a place where the warehouse, the noise, the watching eyes of her coworkers did not exist. She avoided eye contact religiously—looking directly at someone felt like a vulnerability, an exposure. Her belief that her body had betrayed her, that she could not trust her own responses in a crisis, made this numbing feel necessary; by staying blank, by refusing to fully inhabit her own skin, she could avoid the moment when her body might fail her again. If she did not meet their gaze, she reasoned, she could not see the moment their intentions shifted, but more importantly, they could not see into her. These strategies offered temporary relief, a brief reprieve from the exhausting vigilance. Yet each time she dissociated, each time she looked away, she felt her world shrink a little more. The avoidance itself became evidence that danger was real, that her fear was justified. The more she withdrew, the more isolated she became, and the more isolated she became, the more the world seemed hostile and unknowable. By the time she turned twenty-four, she had stopped going to her cousin's gatherings, had turned down a promotion that would have required her to train new staff, and had begun to dread the walk from her car to the warehouse entrance each morning.

Two months ago, a coworker's sudden movement—he had reached past her without warning—sent Mariana into a panic so acute that she left work and did not return for a week. When she finally came back, she knew something had to change. She was failing at the one thing she had managed to hold onto: her job. The thought of losing it terrified her more than anything else, because it would mean admitting that the bomb had taken everything. She called a therapist, hands shaking as she dialed, and when asked what she most wanted to work on, she said, simply, "I need to stop being afraid of everything." What she did not say, but what hung unspoken in the room, was that she did not know if she still knew how.

violations.explanation: Negative appraisals (distorted beliefs about danger and self-blame) are described extensively, and maladaptive strategies (dissociation, avoidance, disconnection) are clearly present, but no paragraph conveys that her negative beliefs directly drive her coping strategies—the causal link is missing.

Threat perception is described throughout, and intrusive memories of the trauma appear, but no paragraph establishes that the sense of threat leads to or triggers the traumatic memory itself—this directional causal relationship is absent.

- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: Negative appraisals (distorted beliefs about danger and self-blame) are described extensively, and maladaptive strategies (dissociation, avoidance, disconnection) are clearly present, but no paragraph conveys that her negative beliefs directly drive her coping strategies—the causal link is missing.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."
- Threat → Memory: Threat perception is described throughout, and intrusive memories of the trauma appear, but no paragraph establishes that the sense of threat leads to or triggers the traumatic memory itself—this directional causal relationship is absent.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
